transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Doctor. Thank you so much for taking the time to see me. Um, I hope I'm explaining this right, I really don't want to waste your time... but I guess what brings me in is that I just can't seem to keep my mind on one thing anymore. 

It's a little embarrassing to admit at my age, honestly, and it's probably not a huge deal, but at the shop... well, if just one saw starts up, or somebody walks past the office, or even if I just have a passing thought about another job, it completely pulls me off what I’m doing. And then, I don't know, the whole day just kind of gets away from me. 

Am I making sense? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right kind of information.
How long have you been experiencing these difficulties with concentration and distractibility? Has this always been a problem for you, or is this something that started more recently?

Oh, um... well, I don't think it's always been quite this bad. I mean, I managed perfectly fine for years when I was just working with my hands. But this... this level of trouble, I guess it’s been going on for about a year and a month now? Give or take? 

I had a little accident and broke my wrist—nothing too serious, just one of those silly things—but because of that, they had to shift me off the actual hands-on carpentry. So now I'm mostly doing the shop paperwork and supervising the other workers. And, well... I guess sitting at a desk just makes it a lot more obvious that my mind wanders. 

Is that the kind of timeline you were looking for? I hope I'm not rambling too much, I just want to make sure I'm answering your question right.
Before you broke your wrist about a year ago, did you ever notice this kind of trouble concentrating or mind-wandering, even when you were doing the hands-on carpentry work?

Well... I mean, when I was working with my hands, it was easier to hide, I suppose. The physical work kind of kept me grounded. But... if I'm being completely honest, and I know I should be... yes, I think it's always been there, creeping in. 

I don't want to sound like I'm making excuses for myself, but even way back when I was a little girl, definitely before I was 12... my teachers were always, always telling my mother the same thing. They'd say I was a bright girl, which was nice of them, but they'd also say I was... well, careless. I'd lose my homework, or I'd forget what they just told us to do. And I spent a lot of time just staring out the window when I was supposed to be doing my seatwork. 

I guess I just learned to work around it when I grew up and started carpentry. Does that make sense? I hope I'm not overcomplicating things by bringing up stuff from so long ago. I just want to give you what you need.

When you're sitting at your desk doing paperwork, do you find yourself fidgeting a lot—like tapping your fingers, bouncing your leg, or having trouble staying still—or is it mainly just your mind wandering while your body is relatively calm?

Well, um... I wouldn't say I'm bouncing off the walls or anything like that. I try really hard to be professional, especially since I'm supervising now. But... I guess if I'm being perfectly honest, it's not just my mind wandering. 

When I have to sit at the desk doing estimates for a long time, or if I'm stuck sitting through a long meeting with the owner, I do get this... well, I feel kind of wound up inside. Like this tight feeling that I just need to get up and move around. Even though my wrist is totally healed now and I know I’m supposed to just stay put and finish the paperwork, it just feels so hard to stay still. I probably shift around in my chair more than I should. 

I hope that doesn't make me sound like a bad employee. I really do try to stay in my seat. Is that the kind of fidgeting you mean, or did I misunderstand the question?

When you were a child in school, besides the mind-wandering and losing things you mentioned, did your teachers or parents ever say you were too restless, fidgety, or had trouble sitting still in class or at home?

Oh, um... well, no, not really. I mean, they never really said I was restless or anything like that. I was always a very quiet girl, you know? I tried my best to be good and not cause any trouble for the teachers. 

I think... I think I mostly just sat there quietly, even if my head was somewhere else. I definitely wasn't one of those kids running around the classroom or disrupting things. I hope that's okay? I just don't remember anyone ever telling my mother that I couldn't sit still, just that I was... well, a bit absent-minded, like I said before. Is that helpful?

When you were a child, did you ever get in trouble for being too talkative, interrupting people, or acting impulsively—like doing things without thinking first—or was it mainly just the daydreaming and forgetfulness?

Oh, goodness, no... I, um, I always tried so hard to be polite. I wouldn't have dared to interrupt a teacher or talk out of turn. I really didn't want to be a bother to anyone, or make anyone upset with me, especially my mother. 

So, no, it was definitely just the... the daydreaming and the forgetfulness, like you said. I would just sit there quietly in my own little world. I hope that's alright? I mean, I hope it doesn't make things too confusing that I wasn't acting out or anything... I just always wanted to be a good girl, even if my head was completely in the clouds. Am I giving you the right kind of information?

When you were a child and teenager, before you started working in carpentry, did you ever feel that wound-up, restless feeling inside that made it hard to sit still—or is that feeling something that only started happening more recently when you began doing desk work?

Oh, um... well, I don't really remember feeling that way when I was younger. I mean, I always tried to be very well-behaved and do what I was told, whether that was at home or sitting in class. I didn't want to be a nuisance or anything. 

I think... I think that tight, wound-up feeling really just started when I began having to do all this paperwork and sitting at a desk for the estimates. When I was just doing the carpentry work, building things with my hands, I was always moving around anyway, so maybe I just didn't notice it? But as a girl... no, I really don't think I felt that way. I hope I'm remembering that right for you. Does that make sense, that it would only start recently with the desk work?

When you were doing the carpentry work with your hands before your wrist injury, even though you were moving around, did you feel like you *needed* to keep moving and staying active to feel comfortable, or was the movement just naturally part of the job itself?

Oh, um... I think it was really just part of the job. I didn't... I didn't feel like I had to keep moving just to feel comfortable, no. It was more that... well, when you're building things, you just naturally have to walk around a lot to get the materials and use the tools. 

I was just doing what the work required of me, you know? I always tried to work hard and do exactly what was needed for the project. So if I had to stand perfectly still to measure something carefully or hold a piece of wood in place, I could do that just fine. It was just the nature of carpentry to be on your feet before my wrist got hurt. 

I hope that's okay? I mean, I hope it's not a bad thing that I didn't feel that restless urge you're talking about... I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right information and not making things too complicated for you. Am I answering that right?

When you were doing carpentry work and had to hold something perfectly still or concentrate on a precise measurement, as you mentioned, did you find it genuinely easy to stay still for those periods, or did you have to push through some internal discomfort to do it?

Oh, no, I... I really think it was genuinely easy for me. I didn't feel any sort of, um, discomfort or anything like that. When I needed to be still to get a measurement exactly right, I just... I just focused and did it. 

I've always taken a lot of pride in my work, you know? Making sure every cut was perfect. So standing still for a minute or two to make sure it was right just felt normal. I didn't have to force myself or fight any kind of urge to move. 

Is that... is that helpful? I hope I'm not making this difficult for you by not having that symptom. I just want to be as honest and helpful as I can be. I'm doing okay, right?

When you were in elementary school, before age 12, did your teachers or parents ever express concern that you were struggling to pay attention in class or having trouble completing assignments—or was the main feedback really just about being careless and daydreaming?

Oh, um... well, yes, I suppose they did say things along those lines. The teachers, I mean. They were always very kind, but even back in grade school, definitely before I was 12, they were always telling my mother that I was bright... which was really sweet of them to say. But... they also said I was a bit careless. 

I feel a little embarrassed even admitting it to you, because I really did try so hard to be a good student, but I was always losing my homework or just... forgetting the instructions they had just given us. And they'd tell my mom that I was staring out the window instead of finishing my seatwork. 

I wasn't trying to be defiant or ignore them, I promise. I just... my mind would drift off, even though I wanted to do well and make them happy. Does that answer your question? I hope I'm giving you the right details. I know it sounds a bit silly for a grown woman to still be embarrassed about grade school, but I just want to make sure I'm doing this right for you. Is that what you meant?

When you were a child, did your parents or teachers ever mention that you seemed to have a lot of energy, or that you were always on the go—like you needed to be doing something or moving around all the time—even if you were trying to be quiet and well-behaved?

Oh, um... no, they never really said anything like that. I was actually a very quiet little girl. I didn't... I didn't run around or have too much energy, no. 

I was always trying so hard to be good and well-behaved, you know? I would just sit quietly at my desk or in my room. If anything, my mother used to say I was almost too quiet, because I'd just be sitting there in my own little world, daydreaming. I never felt that urge to be running around or constantly doing things. 

I really hope that's okay? I know sometimes people think of little kids as being full of energy and bouncing off the walls, but I just wasn't like that. I don't want to mess up your diagnosis by not having that symptom... I'm just trying to give you the most accurate picture I can. Is it alright that I was more on the quiet side?

When you were working in carpentry and moving around all day, did you ever notice that on days when you had to sit down for longer periods—like during lunch breaks, or in the evenings at home—that same wound-up, restless feeling would come back, or is that feeling truly something that only started happening in the past year or so with the desk work?

Oh, um... no, it really is just a recent thing. Back when I was doing my regular hands-on carpentry, I was perfectly fine just sitting and resting during my lunch break or in the evenings. It was actually really peaceful. 

This... this whole level of trouble I've been having, it really has only been going on for about a year and a month. I had a bit of an accident and broke my wrist, you see. My boss was incredibly kind and wanted to keep me on, so they shifted me into doing the shop paperwork and supervising the younger crew instead of my usual hands-on work. 

I've been trying so hard to be good at the desk work, I really have, because I don't want to let them down after they were so nice to me. But that's when all this really started. 

I hope it's okay that it's only been happening for a year and a month? I don't want to sound like I'm complaining about the new position, because I'm very grateful to still be working. I'm just trying to give you the exact timeline like you asked. Am I explaining that alright for you?

Around the time you broke your wrist about a year ago, or shortly after, did you notice any other changes in your health—like changes in your energy level, sleep, appetite, weight, mood, or how you felt physically? Or did anything else happen medically around that same time?

Oh, um... no, not really. I mean, breaking my wrist was quite enough excitement for one year, I think! But no, other than the pain from the break and the cast, I didn't really have any other big changes. 

My sleep and appetite have been pretty much the same as always. I mean, my mood was a little low just because I couldn't do the physical work I love, but I wouldn't say it was anything major. I really tried to keep a positive attitude about it, you know? I didn't want to be a burden to my husband or my boss by moping around. 

Physically, I felt fine, just... adjusting to doing everything with one good hand for a while. There weren't any other medical problems or big health changes. I hope that's the right answer? I know sometimes these things are all connected, but I really want to make sure I'm giving you the right information. Is it okay that nothing else was really going on?
When you broke your wrist about a year ago, were you prescribed any medications—like pain relievers or anything else—that you're still taking now, or did you stop taking them once the wrist healed?

Oh, um... no, nothing like that. They gave me some pills for the pain right at the beginning, of course, because it did ache quite a bit when it first happened. But I stopped taking them as soon as I could. I really don't like taking strong medicine if I can help it, you know? I wanted to be clear-headed for the new paperwork job. 

So, no, I'm not taking anything from back then. I just toughed it out once the worst of it was over. I hope that's what you were looking for? I know some people need to take those things longer, and I'm not judging, but I just wanted to make sure I was doing the right thing by getting off them quickly. Did I handle that okay?

Besides the pain medication you mentioned, have you been diagnosed with any medical conditions in the past year or so—like thyroid problems, anemia, sleep apnea, or anything like that—or have you started taking any other medications or supplements that you're still on now?

Oh, um... no, I haven't. I haven't had to go to the doctor for anything like that at all. No thyroid issues or anemia or anything. And I'm not taking any other pills or supplements, either. 

I try to just eat a decent diet and take care of myself so I don't have to bother the doctors too much, you know? I hope that's alright. I know sometimes a vitamin deficiency or something simple might explain why someone is having a hard time, and it would probably make your job easier if I had something like that to tell you, but I really am completely healthy otherwise. 

Is it okay that I don't have anything else to report for you? I'm trying to be as thorough as I can.

You mentioned that before your wrist injury, you were able to manage fine doing carpentry work even though you had some difficulty concentrating. When you first transitioned to the desk job about a year ago, did the concentration problems and that wound-up feeling start right away, or did they develop gradually over weeks or months after you started the paperwork?

Oh, um... well, it started pretty much right away when they moved me to the desk. I broke my wrist about a year and a month ago, and that's when they shifted me to doing the shop paperwork and supervising instead of the hands-on carpentry. 

I really tried my best to just jump right in and be good at it, you know? I wanted to be helpful and not let anyone down while I couldn't use my tools. But almost immediately, sitting there trying to read invoices and fill out forms... that's when I noticed I just couldn't keep my focus, and I started feeling so antsy. 

So it's been going on for about a year and a month now, at this level anyway. I hope I don't sound like I'm complaining too much about the new job. I know I'm lucky they kept me on while I was healing. Does that make sense, that it would happen right when the job changed? I hope that's the right kind of timeline you're looking for.

When you do have to sit at the desk now, if you take a break and step away for a bit—maybe walk around the shop or get some fresh air—does that help settle that wound-up feeling and make it easier to focus when you come back, or does the restlessness and trouble concentrating come right back even after you've had a break?

Oh, um... well, taking a break does feel nice, of course. I try to get up and stretch my legs or walk out to the floor just to see how the guys are doing. I want them to know I'm still part of the team, you know? 

But... I guess when I sit back down at the desk, it doesn't really fix it. The antsy feeling comes right back pretty much as soon as I look at the paperwork again. It's like I can't shake it, no matter how many little walks I take. I try so hard to just sit still and power through it, because I know that's what I'm supposed to do. I don't want the boss thinking I'm just wandering around avoiding work. 

I really wish the breaks helped more, so I could just come back and focus like a normal person. Is it bad that stepping away doesn't help me settle down? I hope I'm not making it sound like I'm not trying. I really am trying my best to stay on task.
